newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Howard to put native title plan to Aborigines.
newsitem.headline: Howard to put native title plan to Aborigines.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard will on Monday spell out to Aboriginal leaders his plan to settle the bitter dispute over native land title, which farmers and miners say is hurting their industries.

"I am putting forward a government position ... the government position I outlined to the Cabinet last week," he told reporters, adding that he planned no legislative abolition of the Aborigines' newly-won rights to use rural land.
Asked whether a solution was close, he said: "I'll be able to answer that probably more fulsomely later on today after I've met the leaders of the Aboriginal community."

Earlier, the rural-based National Party, a partner in the ruling Liberal-National coalition and always hostile to any loss of farmers' rights, publicly backed the plan that Howard has not yet detailed.
"We are very close to finding a strong and unified approach to it," Deputy National Party Leader and Primary Industries Minister John Anderson said on radio.
The National Party has demanded that parliament simply extinguish the High Court's invention of native rights to pastoralists leases and compensate Aborigines for the loss.
But Anderson did not repeat that demand on Monday and said some other approach might achieve the security for farmers that the National Party had sought.
"But our position is clear, our objectives are clear ...", Anderson said. "We have to have the restoration of the certainty that we're looking for."

Farmers -- and to a lesser extent miners -- have complained that uncertainty has crippled primary industries since the court in December unexpectedly ruled that Aborigines had unspecified rights to land that the government had let to pastoralists.
Howard has been negotiating with both sides since the ruling but has said that if farmers and Aborigines cannot agree then he will impose a solution. He discussed one with Cabinet last week.
Newspapers reported on Monday that a key element of the plan would be to abolish any native title rights that were inconsistent with farmers carrying on pastoral activities.
But the plan would also guarantee access rights to the land for Aborigines.
"What I've put forward does not involve blanket extinguishment," Howard said, describing his plan.
The High Court originally created native title in 1992, overturning the old assumption that Aborigines had owned nothing when the British settlers arrived on the continent in 1788.

The ruling, in the Mabo case, set of a prolonged and bitter dispute in which the former Labor government looked for a way of regulating native title and limiting any economic damage from it without discriminating against Aborigines.
But that settlement assumed that the court would not also impose native land rights on pastoral leases -- so the December Wik ruling has opened up the dispute again.
Howard has said that 78 percent of Australia's 7.68 million square km (2.96 million square miles) of land was "potentially claimable" by Aborigines under native title laws.
